units.t: Mind-Bending Maths. Episode two.
In this episode: Every shuffle is history: the astonishing size of 52, The seven bridges puzzle and the maths of networks and I cut, you choose: the maths of fair sharing.
Part one. Every shuffle is history: the astonishing size of 52.
Shuffle a pack of cards properly and you have almost certainly created an order that no one in history has ever held.
The maths behind that claim is simple and staggering.
Fifty-two factorial.
Three books can be arranged 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways; four, 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.
This multiplying-down pattern is a factorial, written 4!.
Christian Kramp introduced the notation in 1808.
Ten books give 3,628,800 orders, and twenty give more than two quintillion.
For a pack of 52 cards, 52!
is roughly 8 × 10⁶⁷, a number 68 digits long that begins 8065.
Imagine all eight billion people alive today shuffling once a second since the Big Bang, about 13.
8 billion years ago.
They would have made roughly 3.
5 × 10²⁷ decks, less than a billionth of a billionth of a billionth of all possible orders.
Almost certainly a first.
A well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order that has never existed before.
The catch is the word ‘well’.
A new pack comes in set order, and a couple of lazy shuffles leave much of it intact.
Uniqueness applies only when all 52!
orders are equally likely.
How many shuffles is enough?
In 1992 Dave Bayer and Persi Diaconis analysed the riffle shuffle, where you split the deck and let the halves fall together.
The deck stays noticeably ordered at first, then becomes well mixed quite suddenly at around seven shuffles.
More adds little.
The overhand shuffle is far weaker: one analysis suggested thousands.
Diaconis left home as a teenager to travel as a magician before becoming a professor of statistics.
The perfect shuffle.
Skilled magicians can cut a deck into two exact halves of 26 and interleave them perfectly, one card from each side in turn.
In the out-shuffle, the top card stays on top.
Do it once and the deck looks mixed.
Keep going and something surprising happens: after exactly eight perfect out-shuffles, a 52-card deck returns to its original order.
Magicians use this predictability to make a pack look mixed while knowing where every card is.
The lesson is that mixing depends on randomness.
A shuffle that is too precise is just a permutation, a fixed rearrangement, and repeating a fixed rearrangement enough times brings you back to where you began.
When order doesn't matter.
Sometimes order does not matter.
A five-card poker hand is the same hand whatever order you pick the cards up in.
To count hands, start with 52 × 51 × 50 × 49 × 48 ordered ways to deal five cards, then divide by 5!
, the 120 ways of rearranging the same five.
That gives 2,598,960 possible hands.
The same idea measures lotteries.
A game where you choose 6 numbers from 45 has 8,145,060 combinations, so one entry has about a one in eight million chance of the top prize.
This kind of counting is called combinatorics.
It tells you plainly how long the odds are, and why a lottery ticket is entertainment, not a plan.
Why big numbers protect us.
Explosive growth in possibilities protects you every day.
A four-digit PIN has only 10,000 possibilities, which is why banks lock a card after a few wrong guesses.
A long password made of several random words has vastly more, because each extra word multiplies the total.
Modern encryption relies on keys chosen from so many possibilities that trying them all would take longer than the age of the universe, even with enormous computing power.
The same principle that makes a shuffled deck unique makes a properly chosen key unguessable.
The practical takeaway: length and genuine randomness matter far more than clever substitutions, such as swapping the letter o for a zero.
The key idea: A pack of 52 cards can be ordered in about 8 followed by 67 zeros ways, far more than all shuffles ever made.
Part two. The seven bridges puzzle and the maths of networks.
In the 1700s, people in a Prussian city wondered whether they could stroll across all seven of its bridges exactly once.
The answer started a branch of maths that now guides your phone's maps.
A stroll in Königsberg.
The city of Königsberg, in what was then Prussia, sat on the River Pregel.
The river split around two islands, and seven bridges linked the islands to each other and to the two riverbanks.
Residents enjoyed a puzzle: could you walk through the city and cross every bridge exactly once?
You could start and finish anywhere, but no swimming, no boats and no turning back halfway across a bridge.
Nobody could find a route, but nobody could prove none existed.
In 1736 the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler, then working in St Petersburg, took up the problem.
His answer to this small local puzzle launched a whole new field.
Königsberg is now Kaliningrad, part of Russia.
Dots, lines and parity.
Euler threw away almost everything about the map.
Bridge lengths and island shapes made no difference.
Only which land areas connected, and by how many bridges, mattered.
He shrank each land area to a point and each bridge to a line.
Today this diagram is called a graph, with nodes, points, and edges, lines.
This focus on connections grew into graph theory.
Think about passing through a place mid-walk: you arrive by one bridge and leave by another, so bridges are used in pairs.
Only the start and end can have an odd number.
In Königsberg, one island had five bridges and the other three areas had three each.
Four odd points made the walk impossible.
Drawing the house.
Try drawing a house, a square with both diagonals and a triangular roof, without lifting your pen or retracing a line.
Count the lines at each corner.
The top corners of the square have four each and the roof peak has two.
The two bottom corners have three each.
Exactly two odd points means it can be done, but only by starting at one bottom corner and finishing at the other.
Start anywhere else and you get stuck.
Much of old Königsberg was destroyed in the Second World War, and several bridges were lost or replaced.
With the bridges standing today, only two land areas have an odd number, so a walk crossing each exactly once is now possible.
Networks everywhere.
A road map is a graph, with intersections as points and roads as lines labelled with distances or times.
When your phone suggests the fastest route, it is searching a vast graph.
A classic method was devised by the Dutch computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra in 1956, reportedly in about 20 minutes at a café.
Electricity grids, web links and the internet are graphs too.
Social networks are graphs of people.
In the 1960s Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to pass letters towards a target in Boston through acquaintances.
Those that arrived took around six steps, though many never arrived.
In 1998 Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz showed that mostly local friendships plus a few long-range links make 'small worlds'.
A 2016 Facebook analysis found users about 3.
6 steps apart on average.
Four colours suffice.
In 1852 a young British graduate, Francis Guthrie, was colouring a map of England's counties and noticed he never needed more than four colours to keep neighbours different.
Could any map, however complicated, manage with four?
Turn the map into a graph, with regions as points and shared borders as lines, and it becomes a question about networks.
The problem resisted proof for over a century.

In 1976 Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken at the University of Illinois finally proved it, but only by having a computer check nearly two thousand special cases, far too many for a person to do by hand.
Some mathematicians were uneasy about a proof no human could fully check.
Today the theorem is accepted, and computer-assisted proofs are a normal tool.
The key idea: A local puzzle about crossing seven bridges once each launched a new kind of maths.
Part three. I cut, you choose: the maths of fair sharing.
Two children and one cake have a perfect solution that is thousands of years old.
Add more children and mathematicians needed until 2016 to finish the job.
I cut, you choose.
Two siblings, one slice of cake, and an argument brewing.
The classic solution is simple: one cuts, the other chooses.
The cutter has every reason to make the pieces equal in their own eyes, because they get whichever piece is left.
The chooser takes the piece they prefer.
Neither can reasonably complain.
The idea is ancient.
In the Book of Genesis, Abraham proposes dividing the land between himself and Lot, and lets Lot choose.
Mathematicians admire it because it works even when people value things differently.
One sibling may care about the icing and the other about size.
Nobody needs to agree on what fair means or trust anybody else's judgement.
Two kinds of fairness.
A division is proportional if each of n people gets what they consider at least one nth of the total.
It is envy-free if nobody would rather swap their share for another's.
For two people these are the same.
With three or more they differ: you may think you got a fair third yet feel someone else did better.
In the 1940s Hugo Steinhaus, Stefan Banach and Bronisław Knaster devised the last diminisher method.
The first person cuts a slice they think is fair.
Anyone who thinks it too big may trim it, and the last person to trim takes it.
The rest continue with what remains.
It is proportional, but not envy-free.
Three people, then many.
Around 1960 John Selfridge found an envy-free method for three people, and John Conway independently found it in the early 1990s.
It is now called the Selfridge–Conway procedure.
Roughly, the first person cuts three equal pieces.
The second trims the biggest to tie with the second biggest.
The third picks first, the second picks next, and the first takes what remains.
A second round shares the trimmings.
Nobody prefers anyone else's total, in at most five cuts.
For four or more people it was far harder.
In 1995 Steven Brams and Alan Taylor published an envy-free procedure for any number of people, but it had no upper limit on cuts.
In 2016 Haris Aziz and Simon Mackenzie found a bounded method, though it needs astronomically many steps.
It proves fairness is possible, not that it is practical.
Splitting the rent.
Fair division is not just about cake.
Housemates sharing a place with a big sunny room, a small room and a room near the noisy road must divide a rent bill as well as the rooms.
In 1999 the mathematician Francis Su published a method, building on others' work, that uses a result called Sperner's lemma.
It shows there is always a way to set the rents so that each person prefers their own room at its price.
Online tools now use these ideas to split rent, chores and shared costs.
Fairness flips when the thing shared is unpleasant.
With chores, the cutter divides the jobs into two loads they find equally heavy, and the chooser takes the lighter one.
Fairness under the sea.
The most surprising use of divide-and-choose may be international law.

Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, agreed in 1982, a company or country wanting to mine the deep seabed beyond national borders proposes an area large enough for two mining operations, split into two parts of similar estimated value.
The International Seabed Authority then chooses one part to reserve for itself or for developing countries, and the applicant may work the other.
The applicant has every reason to divide fairly, just like the child cutting the cake.
A nursery rule has become a tool of diplomacy, showing that good mechanisms, rather than trust or goodwill, can make sharing work.
The key idea: Divide and choose works because the cutter gets whichever piece is left, so they have every reason to cut fairly.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why does a pack of 52 cards have so many possible orders?
Answer. Choices shrink: 52, then 51, then 50 ….
Question two. What was the Königsberg bridge puzzle?
Answer. Whether one walk could cross all seven bridges once.
Question three. Why does ‘I cut, you choose’ encourage the cutter to be fair?
Answer. The cutter gets whichever piece is left.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
